data.title: The battle tactics of the Magyars and other nomads
data.excerpt: The battle tactics of the Old Hungarians at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries inflicted heavy defeats on the great European armies of the day, and in the end the rulers of the Nitra region and of Moravia succumbed to them as well. Written sources from Plutarch to Leo the Wise describe the same method: shooting from horseback, the feigned flight and an unceasing supply of arrows.
data.metaTitle: The battle tactics of the Magyars and other nomads
data.metaDescription: Shooting from horseback and the feigned flight – the tactics of the Old Hungarians and the nomads, which defeated even the armies of Great Moravia and Nitra.

children.text: The battle tactics of the Old Hungarians at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries inflicted considerable military defeats on the great European armies of the day and lay behind the successful campaigns of conquest of this people, to which in the end our ancestors ruling in the Nitra region and in Moravia also succumbed. Let us therefore look a little more closely at this successful way of fighting.

Other nomadic peoples had battle tactics similar to those of the Hungarians. The oldest account of such a style of fighting describes the way the Parthians fought. A very vivid description by Plutarch records that

“… the Parthians spread out and began to shoot from a distance from all sides. From that moment the Romans were in a difficult position, for even if they stayed in their closed ranks, and even if they wished to advance, they suffered the same losses but inflicted nothing on the enemy. The Parthians struck them and at the same time escaped their missiles. In this skill they were second only to the Scythians. There is perhaps nothing more sensible than, while saving oneself in flight, to defend oneself as well, and thus to rid that flight of its disgrace. As long as the Romans hoped that the Parthians would shoot off their arrows and hold back from the fight, or would decide on close combat, they did not lose their fighting resolve. But when they found that not far off there stood a mass of camels carrying many missiles and arrows, and that the horsemen of the front ranks were taking them from there, Crassus lost his courage, for he could find no way out…”

From the nomads' way of fighting it is clear that a horseman could never carry very many arrows with him, because they would hinder his movement; to replenish them there served above all a standing supply store, which is also mentioned in the quoted passage of Plutarch in connection with the camels.

blocks.alt: The battle tactics of the Magyars and other nomads

children.text: Information on the battle tactics of the Old Hungarians can be gleaned from the works of Maurice, Masudi and Leo the Wise.

These two sources, however, describe the arrangement of the Hungarian battle lines rather differently. According to Leo the Wise their units stood in small groups numbering around 1,000 men. The front line was dense and the units further back were at a short distance from the battle line. The Arab author Masudi writes at the same time about the battle order of the Hungarians and the Pechenegs during their joint attack on Constantinople in 934. Both the Hungarian and the Pecheneg army had a right and a left wing, with the main force in the centre. The Pecheneg side wings consisted of a military unit some 1,000 men strong.

“After they had formed up into battle lines, the mounted units of the right wing struck the main Byzantine units with a hail of arrows. Meanwhile the left wing shifted position. The mounted units of the left wing also rode around and shot at the main Byzantine units with arrows. In the meantime they reached the place from which the mounted units of the right wing had departed. The hail of arrows thus continued and the mounted units turned in a circle like a mill wheel. The Turkish wings and the main force, however, did not move.”

From the continuation it then follows that the task of the Pechenegs was to disrupt the Byzantine battle lines. When the disrupted Byzantine army then launched an attack against the Hungarian main force, which until then had stood calmly, a way was first opened to them and they were covered with a hail of arrows. This cloud of arrows then definitively sealed the fate of the Byzantine army:
“The mounted units appeared from the right and from the left. They had already drawn their swords. The horizon darkened…”
– this is how Masudi ends his description of the fighting.

Even though the two descriptions of the fighting differ from each other, they have something in common. Both battle formations aimed at disrupting and breaking up the dense ranks of the enemy. A special method was the feigned flight: when the opponent attacked, they withdrew and lured him after them, and so tried to disrupt his ranks completely, and as far as possible they strove to avoid a clash. Their main means of combat was the bow and arrows, which allowed them not to wait for an opponent equipped with defensive weapons and spared them from becoming entangled in close combat with an unpredictable outcome.

blocks.alt: The battle tactics of the Magyars and other nomads

children.text: An important part of their tactics, as we have already mentioned above, was securing a sufficient quantity of arrows and their continuous supply during the fighting. The load had to be in the immediate vicinity of the army. If we add up the disrupting, the decimating and the pursuit of the enemy ranks, it is clear that the warriors' quivers, which in themselves had only a very limited capacity, must have been refilled several times. For a mode of attack like a mill wheel, from various sides, they needed countless arrows. It is certain that a given number of horsemen also required a great deal of baggage. It is stated that for every ten men one horse loaded with weapons and provisions was needed. The collection of ammunition took place according to plan, and so each loaded animal was marked to show which unit it belonged to. If we take all these aspects into account, we obtain the picture of an assembled, well-articulated, organised and well-led army.
In the works of Leo the Wise and Maurice it is also possible to find information on weapons and close combat:
“On their shoulders they carried a spear, in their hand they held a bow,”

This claim, however, cannot be proved by the archaeology dealing with the period of the arrival of the Hungarians in the Carpathian Basin. In graves of that period the spear is in fact very rare; officially only about a dozen are recorded. It may therefore be assumed that this part of Maurice refers to the Avars. Spears are indeed characteristic of Avar graves. Their number in a single cemetery equals or exceeds the total number of all the spears found in Hungarian graves. The same applies to the equipment and probably to the armour of the horse, which belong to the Avars. The main weapon of the Hungarians for close combat was the sabre. The sabre of light cavalry, however, could not be used successfully in a close attack against heavily armed mounted troops. The Hungarians therefore avoided this as far as possible.

In the Hungarian defeats during the raids into the west similar knowledge evidently played its part, but for lack of direct sources this can only be assumed. In the battle at Riade (933) the Hungarian army was powerless against heavily armed cavalry. The imperial troops did not scatter but mounted a counter-attack. The feigned flight of the Hungarians turned into real flight. As Widukind writes,
“they took to flight in such a way that within a radius of 8 miles it was not possible to catch or capture anyone”

. But as we learn, they had no other option than flight, because their camp had been occupied by the Germans. Since we already know that the Hungarians had to refill their quivers fairly often in the course of fighting, we can easily understand what a disaster it was for them when all the ammunition kept in the Hungarian camp fell into the hands of the enemy. They therefore had no chance of continuing with their effective method of fighting – defence from a distance. With sabres they could not fight for long against the heavily armed Germans. At Riade part of the Hungarian army was still fortunate and was able to save itself. Perhaps they had not lost all their supply horses and still had enough arrows with which to secure their retreat. In the battle on the Lechfeld (955), however, the Hungarians met a far better prepared opponent. As in the previous case, the Hungarians lost their camp and the possibility of replenishing supplies. With empty quivers they could hardly fight bravely. The well-prepared opponents already knew that Hungarian horsemen were not so dangerous without their arrows. They therefore dared to fight against the fleeing men and annihilated the largest Hungarian army of this raid.

The absolute end of their traditional tactics was brought about by a change in armament. In the army of St Stephen, and perhaps already under Géza, lightly armed mounted units had only a subordinate place. By this time the bow and arrows had been entirely pushed aside in the armament of the Hungarian armies.
